items.readable_text:
Content:
To find the complex conjugate of a complex number, we flip the sign of the imaginary part.

Content:
More precisely, for a complex number [MATH: z=x+\textrm{i}y,] the complex conjugate is denoted [MATH: \overline{z}] and is given by [MATH: \overline{z} = x-\textrm{i}y.]

Content:
Although the complex conjugate is very simple to compute, it has a surprising number of interesting properties that we will learn about in the future.

items.readable_text:
Content:
For a real number, its complex conjugate is always the same as the original number itself.

Content:
To understand why, first notice that any real number [MATH: a] can be expressed as a complex number with an imaginary part of [MATH: 0\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: a = a + 0 \textrm{i}]

Content:
To find the complex conjugate, we need to flip the sign of the imaginary part. So, we get

Content:
[MATH: \overline{a} = a - 0 \textrm{i} = a.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \overline{a} = a.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To find the complex conjugate of a complex number, we flip the sign of the imaginary part.

Content:
More precisely, for a complex number [MATH: z=x+\textrm{i}y,] the complex conjugate is denoted [MATH: \overline{z}] and is given by [MATH: \overline{z} = x-\textrm{i}y.]

Content:
Although the complex conjugate is very simple to compute, it has a surprising number of interesting properties that we will learn about in the future.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Complex Conjugate of a Complex Number With Positive Imaginary Part

What is the complex conjugate of [MATH: z=3+6\textrm{i}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the complex conjugate, we flip the sign of the imaginary part.

In the given number [MATH: z=3+6\textrm{i},] the imaginary part is [MATH: 6\textrm{i}.] Flipping the sign, we get [MATH: -6\textrm{i}.]

Therefore, the complex conjugate is given by [MATH: \overline{z} = 3-6\textrm{i}.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Complex Conjugate of a Real Number

Content:
For a real number, its complex conjugate is always the same as the original number itself.

Content:
To understand why, first notice that any real number [MATH: a] can be expressed as a complex number with an imaginary part of [MATH: 0\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: a = a + 0 \textrm{i}]

Content:
To find the complex conjugate, we need to flip the sign of the imaginary part. So, we get

Content:
[MATH: \overline{a} = a - 0 \textrm{i} = a.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \overline{a} = a.]

Explanation:
The number [MATH: z=-6] is a real number, and the complex conjugate of any real number is just the number itself.

So here, the complex conjugate is [MATH: \overline{z} = z = -6.]
